performed_via_github_app.description:
Codecov provides highly integrated tools to group, merge, archive and compare coverage reports. Whether your team is comparing changes in a pull request or reviewing a single commit, Codecov will improve the code review workflow and quality.

## Code coverage done right.®

1. Upload coverage reports from your CI builds.
2. Codecov merges all builds and languages into one beautiful coherent report.
3. Get commit statuses, pull request comments and coverage overlay via our browser extension.

When Codecov merges your uploads it keeps track of the CI provider (inc. build details) and user specified context, e.g. `#unittest` ~ `#smoketest` or `#oldcode` ~ `#newcode`. You can track the `#unittest` coverage independently of other groups. [Learn more here](
http://docs.codecov.io/docs/flags)

Through **Codecov's Browser Extension** reports overlay directly in GitHub UI to assist in code review in [Chrome](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/codecov/gedikamndpbemklijjkncpnolildpbgo) or Firefox (https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/codecov/)

*Highly detailed* **pull request comments** and *customizable* **commit statuses** will improve your team's workflow and code coverage incrementally.

**File backed configuration** all through the `codecov.yml`. 

## FAQ
- Do you **merge multiple uploads** to the same commit? **Yes**
- Do you **support multiple languages** in the same project? **Yes**
- Can you **group coverage reports** by project and/or test type? **Yes**
- How does **pricing** work? Only paid users can view reports and post statuses/comments.

body: Thanks @Felipegalind0 for your contribution. This PR is quite complex and it took me some time to understand what it does and how. For everyone, including my future self, the idea is to make wheels independent bodies from the aircraft. At its very core, JSBSim assumes that the aircraft is a single body and that other bodies are only interacting with the aircraft through the forces and moments that they apply to it. This is typically the case for propellers where `FGPropeller` is inheriting from `FGForce` via the `FGThruster` class: https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/propulsion/FGPropeller.h#L169 https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/propulsion/FGThruster.h#L77 The class `FGPropeller` manages its own body (the propeller!): * The propeller rotation rate is updated using its inertia and the angular momentum $I\dot{\theta}=\sum_i M_i$: https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/propulsion/FGPropeller.cpp#L294 * Forces and moments are computed and applied to the aircraft: https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/propulsion/FGPropeller.cpp#L282 https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/propulsion/FGPropeller.cpp#L300 The idea of the PR is to apply the same logic to the wheels using `FGLGear`: they become independent bodies with their own degree of freedom (DOF) and they apply a force and a moment to the aircraft. Above are free body diagrams of the wheel: the friction force $F_{\text{roll}}$ is the friction that the ground applies to the wheel and that the wheel applies to the aircraft axle (point A). Hence - now that the wheel is an independent body - the friction force is applied on the aircraft at the point A instead of the point C, so the code below is updated by the PR: https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/FGLGear.cpp#L725 Note that in this PR, $F_{\text{roll}}$ is used for 2 different purposes: 1. To apply the friction force to the aircraft body (as is currently the case) 2. To compute the driving torque $R\cdot F_{\text{roll}}$ (in blue on the picture above) that will be applied to the wheel. ### Braking management Unlike in the current code, the friction coefficient for $F_{\text{roll}}$ is always the static coefficient $\mu_{\text{static}}$ and is independent of the brake position `BrakePos`. To keep the braking feature, the patch introduces the braking torque $\tau_{brake}$ (in yellow on the picture above) that is currently not modeled by `FGLGear`. Hence the new Lagrange multiplier `ftWheelBrake` whose job is to zero out the relative motion between the wheel and the aircraft. The braking torque $\tau_{brake}$ obviously depends on the brake position `BrakePos` and is using `BrakeFCoeff`: https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/FGLGear.cpp#L590-L593 It is following that the wheel applies permanently a resisting torque $\mu_{\text{rolling}}F_{\text{roll}}R$ to the axle, whatever the braking position and this has 2 consequences: 1. The rolling friction coefficient is now characterizing the friction between the wheel and its axle. Legacy behavior is to assume that the rolling friction coefficient characterizes the hysteresis in the compression/expansion of the tire while rolling. There is nothing problematic in these two different interpretations of the rolling friction coefficient but model designers need to know that. 2. When the wheel is spinning $\tau_{\text{brake}}$ will **always** be equal to the maximum torque allowed by the Coulomb law i.e. $\tau_{\text{brake}}=\mu_{\text{brake}}F_{\text{roll}}R$ because the `ftWheelBrake` multiplier is targetting a *no wheel spin* condition. So, how is braking working, now? When applying some brake, $\tau_{brake}$ increases, $\omega$ decreases so $F_{\text{roll}}$ increases to try to restore the no slip condition $R\omega=v_A$. Note that $F_{\text{roll}}$ can reach $\mu_{\text{static}}F_n$ with the wheel still spinning. ### Wheel dynamics The driving torque and the braking torque are then used to compute the spin rate $\omega$ using the classic angular momentum equation $$I\dot{\omega}=R\cdot F_{\text{roll}}-\tau_{\text{brake}}$$ Note that there is a subtlety here: $\omega$ is the wheel spin rate **measured in the NED frame** (so-called *absolute spin rate* in the PR). This is deviating from what most people would expect i.e. a spin rate measured in the body frame: * This allows to define the no slip condition as $R\omega=V_{\text{axle}}$ instead of $R\omega=V_C$ where $V_C$ is the velocity at the contact point with respect to the ground (i.e. $V_C=V_G+\Omega_{\text{aircraft}}\times GC$). It simplifies the code a bit but; * The condition that the `ftWheelBrake` multiplier has to resolve is not $\omega=0$ but $$\omega=\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}\cdot\vec{u}_{\text{axle}}$$ ### No slip condition vs *no wheel spin* condition With respect to that point, the code in the PR is not so easy to understand because it is far from obvious that, for the `ftWheelBrake` multiplier, the following code actually simplifies to the equation above: ```c++ double wheelTerm = (mi->Wheel && dt > 0.) ? mi->WheelCoeff * mi->Wheel->Rate / dt : 0.; rhs[i] = -(DotProduct(U, vdot) + DotProduct(moment(mi), wdot) + wheelTerm)/d; ``` As a reminder, according to the following code: https://github.com/JSBSim-Team/jsbsim/blob/14c19022943f5850daf2c6b90554050b3139b853/src/models/FGAccelerations.cpp#L265-L273 we have (the terrain movement is ignored to simplify the analysis) $$\text{vdot}=\dfrac{d\vec{v}_G}{dt}+\dfrac{\vec{v}_G}{\Delta t}$$ $$\text{wdot}=\dfrac{d\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}}{dt}+\dfrac{\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}}{\Delta t}$$ So, for `ftWheelBrake`, we have $U=0$, `moment(mi)` is equal to $-u_{\text{axle}}$, `mi->WheelCoeff == 1.0`, and `mi->Wheel->Rate` is obviously $\omega$ so we have: $$\text{rhs}=\left(-\dfrac{d\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}}{dt}\cdot\vec{u}_{\text{axle}}+\dfrac{\omega-\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}\cdot\vec{u}_{\text{axle}}}{\Delta t}\right)\dfrac{1}{d}$$ where one can recognize the *no wheel spin* condition $\omega-\Omega_{\text{aircraft}}\cdot u_{\text{axle}}$ *Note: You can ignore the time derivation and the division by `d` because they are technical details unrelated to the point I am trying to make.* On the other hand, for the `ftRoll` multiplier, the same C++ code leads to the no slip condition because $U=u_{\text{roll}}$, `moment(mi)` is equal to $GA\times u_{\text{roll}}$ and `mi->Wheel->Rate` is equal to $-R$ so we have $$\text{rhs}=\left(\vec{u}_{\text{roll}}\cdot\left(\dfrac{d\vec{v}_G}{dt}+\dfrac{\vec{v}_G}{\Delta t}\right)+(\vec{GA}\times\vec{u}_{\text{roll}})\cdot\left(\dfrac{d\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}}{dt}+\dfrac{\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}}{\Delta t}\right)+\dfrac{-R\omega}{\Delta t}\right)\dfrac{1}{d}$$ which simplifies to (using the identity $(A\times B)\cdot C=(C\times A)\cdot B$) $$\text{rhs}=\left(\vec{u}_{\text{roll}}\cdot\left(\dfrac{d\vec{v}_G}{dt}+\dfrac{d\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}}{dt}\times\vec{GA}\right)-\dfrac{R\omega-\vec{u}_{\text{roll}}\cdot(\vec{v}_G+\vec{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}\times\vec{GA})}{\Delta t}\right)\dfrac{1}{d}$$ and since the velocity at the axle is $v_A=v_G+{\Omega}_{\text{aircraft}}\times GA$, we finally have: $$\text{rhs}=\left(\vec{u}_{\text{roll}}\cdot\dfrac{d\vec{v}_A}{dt}-\dfrac{R\omega-\vec{u}_{\text{roll}}\cdot\vec{v}_A}{\Delta t}\right)\dfrac{1}{d}$$ where we recognize the no slip condition $R\omega-u_{\text{roll}}\cdot v_A$. So, great! the code works. However it has been a pain to understand that this code covers two entirely different conditions using some tricks: setting $U$ to 0 and the not-very-well-named `WheelCoeff` to either 1 or $-R$! ### Conclusion (for now) As claimed, the PR brings a better and more realistic handling of braking, wheel spin up energy, wheel spin up when touching ground, etc. However, the code deserves some clean up and there are a couple of errors that need to be addressed. To be continued... (sorry I'm running out of time for now but questions/comments on my analysis above are welcome).

Merci beaucoup @bcoconni for the addition of your writeup. In an ideal world every non-trivial bit of physics code in JSBSim would include a URL in the class/method pointing to writeups like this, i.e. markdown/jupyter style with snippets of explanatory text, equations, diagrams, snippets of code.
